strengths: Rigorously proves fundamental limitation of existing methods with three well-constructed theorems showing posterior mean, Gaussian, and guidance scale approximations are inherently biased
Proposes theoretically justified consistent estimators with formal convergence guarantees; Equations 16 and 20 are proven to converge to true diffused likelihood as K→∞
Comprehensive experimental validation on Bayesian inference benchmark with ground truth posteriors, clearly demonstrating CBG improves with compute while baselines plateau
Non-obvious variance analysis (Section 5.3) revealing REINFORCE estimator has lower variance than gradient-based despite conventional wisdom, with intuitive explanation via weighted averaging
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figure 1) illustrating core insight; well-organized progression from problem identification to solutions
weaknesses: Solutions (reparameterization trick, REINFORCE) are standard techniques—novelty lies primarily in identifying where to apply them rather than developing fundamentally new methods

Severe computational limitation inadequately addressed: 2h40 per image on H100 is prohibitively expensive; paper mentions few-step models as solution but doesn't implement it; no scaling analysis for high-dimensional problems
Marginal improvements on real task: black hole imaging shows 26.10 vs 25.86 PSNR over DPS—improvement within noise margin; method matches rather than beats SOTA

Experimental design fairness issues: CBG doesn't tune guidance scale γ while baselines do, making it unclear if improvements stem from calibration or hyperparameter search avoidance; gradient-based CBG performs poorly on 3 of 5 benchmark tasks with large std deviations

Insufficient practical guidance: paper doesn't quantify when calibration matters vs is unnecessary; recommends K and M without principled selection criteria; gradient-based vs gradient-free choice lacks clear guidance despite vastly different performance

Missing ablations: no comparison of biased methods given matching computational budget; no analysis of what happens to biased methods with greatly increased K; unclear if marginal gains justify 2h40 cost
Regularity assumptions glossed over: Theorem 4.1 Lipschitz requirement and tail behavior discussion insufficient; no analysis of sharp likelihood scenarios where self-normalization might fail
Incomplete end-to-end analysis: convergence from correct intermediate p(xt|y) to true p(x|y) assumed rather than proven; no finite-sample convergence rates or practical sample complexity analysis

strengths: Rigorous theoretical analysis proving that existing guidance methods produce biased posterior estimates (Theorems 4.1-4.3 with sound mathematical proofs)
Clear identification and exposition of an important gap in the literature regarding calibration of Bayesian posteriors in diffusion models
Comprehensive experimental benchmark on 5 diverse Bayesian inference tasks with measurable improvements in distributional fit (C2ST)
Practical solutions handling both differentiable and non-differentiable reward functions
Well-motivated problem setup with effective visual illustration of the calibration failure (Figure 1)
weaknesses: Prohibitive computational cost undermines practical utility: 2h40 per image on H100 for black hole imaging with only marginal 0.24 dB PSNR improvement over DPS, yet true wall-clock time comparisons missing from main results

Limited novelty in proposed solutions: Equation (16) is standard reparameterization trick; Equation (20) is REINFORCE (1992). Contribution is primarily applying known techniques rather than methodological innovation

Unclear when practitioners should use CBG: paper acknowledges that for natural images quality matters more than calibration, but for scientific applications (black hole imaging) empirical gains are negligible, leaving the core motivation underdeveloped

Unfair experimental comparisons: different hyperparameter budgets across methods (Table 3-4), constraint N·K≤10^5 obscures computational differences, no sensitivity analysis for K, missing wall-clock time measurements
Limited experimental scope: all Bayesian inference tasks low-dimensional (≤10D), no high-dimensional or realistic imaging experiments, only two qualitative examples for black hole task

Thin theoretical analysis of proposed method: no convergence rates, finite-sample complexity, or bias-variance trade-offs for CBG; Section 5.3 claims gradient-free has lower variance contradicting standard theory with only one toy example (Appendix C)

Missing practical guidance: no analysis of when calibration substantially improves downstream task performance, what problem dimensions justify the computational cost, or how to choose sampling budget K
Concurrent work (Potaptchik et al. 2026) implementing similar ideas suggests limited novelty advantage

strengths: Rigorous theoretical contributions: Theorems 4.1-4.3 rigorously prove that existing guidance methods yield biased estimators that remain biased asymptotically, providing fundamental insights into a widely-used framework
Strong validation of consistency claim: Figure 3 convincingly shows CBG improves with increased compute while baselines plateau, directly validating the core theoretical claim

Principled solution framework with practical variants: Two estimators (gradient-based and gradient-free) provide flexibility; gradient-free variant elegantly handles non-differentiable objectives without computing model/likelihood gradients

Comprehensive experimental design: Bayesian Inference Benchmark substantially outperforms baselines (avg C2ST 0.527 vs. 0.803 for DPS) and comparisons include both diffusion-based and likelihood-free methods across 5 diverse tasks

Clear presentation and honest limitations discussion: Paper is well-written with effective visualizations; authors transparently acknowledge computational cost and discuss potential solutions (few-step diffusion models)
Sound mathematical proofs: Theorems use appropriate techniques (Taylor expansion with positive definite covariance, convolution theorem, Jensen's inequality) and are verified to be correct
weaknesses: Prohibitive computational cost severely limits practical adoption: Black hole imaging requires 2h40 per image on H100 GPU; requires K inner-loop samples at each of N timesteps (O(NM) cost). While pretraining few-step models is mentioned, it is not demonstrated

Marginal improvements on realistic tasks undermine value proposition: Black hole imaging shows only ~0.03 PSNR improvement over SOTA (26.10 vs. 26.07); no experiments on standard inverse problems with learned diffusion priors; improvement ratios do not justify 100× computational overhead

Gradient-based estimator practically infeasible: Table 1 shows substantial underperformance (0.681 vs. 0.527 avg C2ST); Section 5.3 analysis is limited to 1D toy case; high-dimensional behavior and self-normalization properties uncharacterized; authors explicitly avoid it for experiments

Insufficient evidence that calibration provides practical benefits: Even for scientific application (black hole imaging), realistic gains are negligible; no experiments on tasks where miscalibration demonstrably harms decisions; authors acknowledge natural images prioritize quality over calibration—a major application domain

Theoretical gaps in practical guidance: No convergence rate analysis; no finite-sample bounds on bias-variance tradeoff; unclear when K=1000 vs. K=100 is sufficient; Theorem 4.1 assumes Lipschitz prior and twice-differentiable likelihood (restrictive)

Limited experimental scope reduces generalizability: Bayesian Inference Benchmark uses only closed-form priors/likelihoods; no experiments on large-scale learned diffusion priors (e.g., ImageNet-scale models); black hole imaging uses only 100 test samples; hyperparameter selection (Table 4) shows high variance across tasks with vague justification

Hyperparameter selection lacks principled guidance: K ranges 100-10,000, M ranges 50-1000 across tasks with only 'trade-off between computational effort and image results' justification; sensitivity analysis missing; artificial N·K ≤ 10^5 budget restriction differs from practical tuning

Incremental estimator novelty: Reparameterization trick and REINFORCE are classical techniques; main contribution is application to diffused likelihood—important but somewhat incremental given strong theoretical contributions

strengths: Identifies and rigorously proves fundamental bias in existing guidance methods (Theorems 4.1, 4.3) - a real and important gap in the literature
Proposes consistent estimators (Eqs. 16, 20) that converge to true posterior with increased computational budget, unlike existing methods
Comprehensive theoretical analysis with clear proofs and concrete counterexamples (Example 4.2) establishing when/why common approximations fail
Demonstrates effectiveness across diverse domains: Bayesian inference benchmark (all 5 tasks), black hole imaging (new SOTA 27.08 PSNR), image problems
Practical framework supporting both differentiable and non-differentiable rewards with gradient-free and gradient-based variants
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (Figures 1-2) and honest discussion of limitations including measure-zero manifold failure cases
Solid empirical validation showing monotonic improvement with computational budget (Figures 3, 5) and complete bias reduction (Figure 8)
weaknesses: Computational cost prohibitively high despite being main motivation: DDPM variant ~23 hours/image, renoise variant still 2.9 min for K=512; DPS baseline 24s makes practical adoption unlikely
Core theoretical contribution undermined by heuristic renoising trick (Eq. 21) - acknowledged as heuristic with no error analysis, contradicting the 'principled' framing of the work

Image domain results mixed and difficult to interpret: trails on perceptual metrics (LPIPS 0.298 vs NDTM 0.158, Table 5) due to different prior model (pMF vs classifier-guided), making contribution unclear

Limited methodological novelty: gradient-free is standard importance weighting, gradient-based uses standard reparameterization trick; main contribution is problem identification rather than novel techniques
Important practical limitation unresolved: method fails when likelihood concentrates on measure-zero manifold; proposed solution (manifold projection) deferred as out of scope
Incomplete variance analysis: Section 5.4 claims gradient-free superiority but Figure 7 shows gradient-based better early-time; analysis limited to single example in Appendix C
Bayesian inference benchmark relatively simple (x dimension ≤10, y dimension ≤4×2); unclear if results generalize to higher-dimensional realistic problems
Different priors and schedules across experiments limit generalizability; no ablation studies on hyperparameter sensitivity despite Tables 3-4 showing varied selections across tasks

strengths: Rigorous theoretical analysis proving that existing guidance methods (posterior mean approximation, guidance scaling) are fundamentally biased and fail to sample correct posteriors even with infinite compute; Theorems 4.1 and 4.3 provide non-trivial insights
Clear problem identification with effective visualization (Figure 1) and concrete counterexamples (Example 4.2)
Mathematically principled framework using standard estimators (reparameterization, REINFORCE) to achieve consistency in gradient-based and gradient-free variants
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 15+ baselines, 5 Bayesian tasks, scientific imaging, and image inverse problems with consistent improvements on calibration metrics (C2ST)
Practical approximations including renoising trick (Eq. 21) for computational tractability with one-step models
Well-written paper with clear exposition and honest discussion of limitations
weaknesses: Critical theory-practice gap: theoretical consistency guarantees assume exact p(x|xt) sampling, but all experiments use heuristic renoising approximation (Eq. 21); no theoretical analysis of renoising error or whether consistency is preserved—undermines main contribution

Severe computational cost renders method impractical: 30-1000× slower than baselines (CBG+DDPM takes 23 hours vs DPS 24 seconds for black hole imaging; per-image super-resolution ~74 seconds vs seconds for baselines); even renoise variant takes 2.9 min vs seconds

Weak empirical results on practical problems: black hole imaging shows 0.03 dB PSNR improvement (26.10 vs 26.07 for PnP-DM) at same cost, not supporting SOTA claims; super-resolution uses different prior (pMF vs classifier-guided) making comparison unfair, with worse perceptual metrics (LPIPS 0.298 vs 0.158 for NDTM)

Renoising approximation inadequately justified: described as heuristic with minimal validation; Appendix C provides limited evidence of equivalence to DDPM; this is the key practical contribution but lacks rigorous justification

Unresolved guidance scale problem: Theorem 4.3 proves naive scaling fails, but proposed solution (applying integral at test time or using tempered models) doesn't address practitioners' need to adjust γ post-hoc
Limited applicability: acknowledged measure-zero manifold limitation affects many practical inverse problems (inpainting, constrained generation); paper provides no solution

Methodological novelty limited: gradient-based estimator is standard reparameterization trick; gradient-free is textbook REINFORCE; main novelty is problem identification, not methodological innovation

Experimental concerns: Bayesian benchmark uses artificial closed-form analytic priors unlike typical deep learning settings; super-resolution improvements in PSNR not supported by perceptual metrics (LPIPS, FID); baseline methods not designed for calibration metric

Missing analysis: no error bounds for renoising approximation; unexplained failure of gradient-based method on some tasks (Table 1 Task 5: 0.852 vs 0.525 C2ST); limited exploration of variance-bias tradeoffs

Theory-practice gap not adequately addressed in main text; important details (variance comparison Figure 7) relegated to appendix; connection between theoretical results and practical performance unclear

strengths: Identifies and rigorously proves fundamental inconsistency in existing diffusion guidance methods (Theorems 4.1, 4.3); this is an important theoretical contribution with practical implications

Proposes principled solution with consistent estimators that converge to true posterior with increasing computational budget; both gradient-based and gradient-free variants are theoretically well-motivated

Comprehensive experimental validation: Bayesian inference benchmark shows clear improvements over strong baselines (DPS, LGD, DPG, SCG); Figure 3 and Table 1 demonstrate consistent advantage across diverse tasks
Sets new SOTA PSNR on black hole imaging (27.08 dB); includes evaluation on likelihood-free methods providing broader context
Well-executed theory: elegant proofs using exponential family properties, concrete counterexample (Example 4.2), clear distinction between inconsistent and consistent estimators
Practical efficiency contributions: renoising trick (Eq. 21) enables tractable computation; tiled decomposition for high-dimensional problems; leverages existing one-step models
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (especially Figure 1-2) showing failure modes of existing methods and how CBG recovers true posterior
Figure 8 provides valuable bias-variance decomposition confirming that CBG methods converge to correct solution while existing methods plateau at biased value
weaknesses: Computational cost severely limits practical applicability: black hole imaging takes ~6 hours with K=65536 vs 24s for DPS; super-resolution requires 16,384 model evaluations per image; gradient-based variant requires expensive backpropagation through sampling

Theory-practice gap: renoising trick (Eq. 21) is heuristic with no theoretical analysis of introduced bias; empirical validation is limited to black hole imaging; unclear when one-step approximation maintains consistency guarantees

Limited guidance on practical hyperparameter selection: no principled approach for choosing K; computational cost grows linearly with K but guidance is only 'use more compute'; tiling approach for super-resolution appears ad-hoc and task-specific

Variance analysis is informal: Section 5.4 intuition about gradient-free advantages is reasonable but Figure 7 shows task/region-dependent behavior; high-dimensional variance analysis limited to toy 1D example in Appendix C

Experimental fairness issues in super-resolution: uses different prior (pixel mean flow) than baselines (classifier-guided) making direct SOTA claims problematic; trails on perceptual metrics (LPIPS, FID) despite PSNR advantage
Missing robustness analysis: no evaluation of how poor p(x|xt) approximation or prior mismatch affects posterior calibration; measure-zero manifold limitation identified but not resolved

Limited scope of realistic applications: Bayesian inference benchmark uses analytic (Gaussian/Uniform) priors which are artificial; only ~100 black hole imaging instances; image inverse problems mostly qualitative
Concurrent work (Potaptchik et al. 2026) proposes training few-step models for similar estimators, somewhat diminishing novelty; suggests the core idea is becoming standard
